# Maximum-volume-stratum centroid graph and intrinsic transfer

This note proves OC for equal positive intrinsic-volume fibers, in all
integer and continuous dimensions. It also proves a maximum-fiber-mass
bound for every mixed convex body. The equal-volume assumption in the
first consequence is essential to its stated scope; the note does not
prove general OC for unequal fibers.

The classical ingredients used below are the Brunn--Minkowski theorem
and its equality case for positive-volume convex bodies, ordinary
Grunbaum at a convex body's centroid, and Doignon's Helly theorem for
Z^n. Every additional graph, measure, degeneracy and transfer assertion
is proved explicitly. No mixed-integer Grunbaum assertion is invoked.

## Theorem

Let n,d>=0 with n+d>=1. Let C be a convex body in R^n x R^d and let

    S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d)

be nonempty. For every nonempty fiber K_z=C_z, let its affine dimension
be dim K_z. Set

    q=max_z dim K_z=dim_H S,
    a_z=H_q(K_z), M=sum_z a_z=H_q(S),
    a=max_z a_z>0,
    P_max={z:a_z=a}, M_max=a |P_max|.

The H_q on a fiber is the usual intrinsically normalized Hausdorff
measure in its affine span; H_0 counts points. Let

    gamma_0=1, gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r for r>=1.

There exists an actual point y in a maximum-volume fiber such that
EVERY closed halfspace H of the full ambient space containing y obeys

    H_q(S intersect H)>=(gamma_q/2^n) M_max.          (1)

Thus the normalized depth is at least

    (gamma_q/2^n)(M_max/M)
       >=(gamma_d/2^n)(M_max/M).                    (2)

For q=d, the equal-positive-volume consequence is already accepted fact e4253a0d6f78849c. The additional content submitted here is the maximal-stratum mass bound and the intrinsic q-dimensional extension, keeping zero-measure fibers in the underlying set.

## 1. Measure and intrinsic centroids

Boundedness of C gives finitely many nonempty integer fibers. Each is
compact and convex. A nonempty convex set of affine dimension r has
positive finite H_r measure when it is bounded: it contains an
r-simplex in its affine span, and lies in a bounded set there. Its
H_q measure is zero when r<q. Hausdorff dimension of a finite union
is the maximum of the dimensions. Since the fibers lie in mutually
disjoint parallel integer sections, finite Borel additivity gives

    H_q(S)=sum_z H_q(K_z), 0<M<infinity.

For q=0 every nonempty fiber is a singleton, a_z=1 and M is the
number of nonempty fibers. For q>0 the positive a_z are exactly those
fibers of dimension q. Hence a>0 is attained and P_max is finite and
nonempty in all cases.

For z in P_max let

    g_z=(1/a) integral_(K_z) x dH_q(x)

be its intrinsic centroid. When q=0 this is its only point. In every
case g_z belongs to K_z. Define the finite centroid set and its hull

    T={(z,g_z):z in P_max}, G=conv(T).                (3)

Since every point of T lies in C, the compact convex set G lies in C.

## 2. A maximum-volume equality lemma, including changing affine spans

Suppose z_1,...,z_m are in P_max, all weights lambda_i are positive,
sum lambda_i=1, and w=sum lambda_i z_i is an integer vector. Then

    w in P_max,
    sum_i lambda_i g_(z_i)=g_w.                      (4)

Zero weights can be deleted, so positivity causes no restriction on
an arbitrary finite convex representation.

To prove this, convexity of C gives

    L=sum_i lambda_i K_(z_i) subset K_w.             (5)

If q=0, every original nonempty integer fiber is a singleton. The
left side is the singleton with point sum lambda_i g_(z_i), so K_w
is that same singleton, a_w=1=a, and (4) follows.

Suppose q>=1. Put V_i=lin(K_(z_i)-K_(z_i)); each V_i has dimension q.
The direction space of the affine hull of a Minkowski sum is the sum
of the direction spaces, so

    affdim L=dim(V_1+...+V_m).

Indeed affine hull commutes with Minkowski sums; equivalently, holding
all but one summand fixed gives each V_i among the directions of the
sum, and the reverse containment is immediate. Since L is contained
in the integer fiber K_w, whose affine dimension is at most q, this
dimension is at most q. It is at least q because it contains V_1.
Thus all V_i are the SAME q-dimensional linear space V, and K_w also
has affine direction V. This step rules out an untracked increase in
fiber dimension, without assuming that different original fibers had
parallel intrinsic affine spans.

Translate the bodies into V and apply q-dimensional Brunn--Minkowski:

    H_q(L)^(1/q)>=sum_i lambda_i a^(1/q)=a^(1/q).

But H_q(K_w)<=a by definition of the maximum, while (5) gives the
opposite inequality. Therefore all volumes are a. In particular w
belongs to P_max, and L=K_w. The equality of sets follows from the
following elementary fact: a proper inclusion of full-dimensional
compact convex bodies in the same affine space strictly increases
volume. To verify that fact, separate a point of the larger body
outside the smaller one, and take sufficiently small convex mixtures
of that point with an interior ball of the larger body. This produces
a positive-radius ball outside the smaller body and inside the larger
one, contradicting equality of volumes.

Equality in Brunn--Minkowski forces all the source bodies to be
homothetic in V. Because their volumes are equal, they are translates.
For more than two summands this follows by induction: group one body
against the normalized Minkowski average of the others. Both steps
of the Brunn--Minkowski lower bound must be equalities, and the grouped
average also has volume a. The two-body equality theorem and the
induction then give translations of all bodies. In dimension one,
the same assertion follows directly because intervals of the same
length are translates.

Write K_(z_i)=K_0+t_i for one body K_0 and translation vectors t_i in
R^d. Its Minkowski average is K_0+sum lambda_i t_i, so its centroid is
exactly sum lambda_i g_(z_i). Since L=K_w, this is g_w. This proves
(4). No general additivity of centroids under Minkowski sums is used;
it is used only after translations have been established.

## 3. Every integer section of G is one centroid

For any (w,x) in G with w integer, a convex representation in (3)
satisfies the hypotheses of Section 2 after deleting zero weights.
Equation (4) yields w in P_max and x=g_w. Conversely every centroid
point of T belongs to G. Therefore

    G intersect (Z^n x R^d)=T,                      (6)

and every nonempty integer fiber of G is a singleton. In particular
P_max is lattice convex: conv(P_max) intersect Z^n=P_max.

This also explains why zero- or smaller-volume fibers introduce no
hidden integer projection points into the centroid hull. A convex
average of maximum-dimensional positive fibers at an integer base
must itself have dimension at least q and volume at least a, hence
must be a maximum fiber. No lower-dimensional boundary fiber is
silently removed to justify (6).

## 4–5. Existing finite-graph Helly and centerpoint input

Put N=|P_max|=|T|. The preceding section proves that G=conv(T) has exactly the indicated singleton integer sections. In particular T is closed under the admissible same-parity midpoints. Accepted fact bee3cc8e50a0dcea supplies h(T)<=2^n. Applying the closed-halfspace centerpoint argument in accepted fact 6d6fcf377e68c79c to counting measure on T selects one actual t=(z,g_z) in T for which every closed ambient halfspace H containing t contains at least |P_max|/2^n graph points. In the notation used below,

    |T intersect H| >= N/2^n for every closed H containing t.                         (7)

For n=0, T is a singleton and the claim is immediate. For d=0 and n>0, embed T as (z,0) in one extra unused continuous coordinate and apply the same graph theorem; restricting its conclusion to lifted original halfspaces gives the required assertion. This is reused background. The new maximal-stratum/intrinsic transfer is in the following section.

## 6. Transfer counting depth back to original fiber measure

Choose y from Sections 4–5, which is (w,g_w) in a maximum fiber and thus
belongs to the original S. Fix any closed ambient halfspace H
containing it. For each centroid point (z,g_z) in T intersect H,
restrict H to the affine span of K_z. If its defining normal has
nonzero restriction there, the restriction is a closed q-dimensional
halfspace containing g_z, and ordinary Grunbaum gives

    H_q(K_z intersect H_z)>=gamma_q a.

If the restriction is constant, the entire fiber is contained because
its centroid is contained, so its mass a obeys the same lower bound.
For q=0 this is simply the counting contribution of the contained
singleton and gamma_0=1. Thus fiber-parallel and oblique halfspaces,
including those containing an entire boundary fiber, are all covered.

Summing the contributions of the centroids counted in (7), and then
retaining the nonnegative contribution of every other original fiber,
gives

    H_q(S intersect H)
       >=gamma_q a |T intersect H|
       >=(gamma_q/2^n)aN.

This is (1). Finally gamma_r decreases with positive integer r:
x log(1+1/x) has positive derivative
log(1+1/x)-1/(x+1), so (1+1/r)^r increases. With gamma_0=1 this gives
gamma_q>=gamma_d for 0<=q<=d and proves (2).

## 7. Boundary cases and limitations

- If d=0, all fibers are points, q=0, a=1 and M_max=M. Sections 3--5
  give the counting centerpoint bound 2^(-n), with gamma_0=1.
- If n=0, there is one fiber, and Section 6 is ordinary Grunbaum.
- If q=0 with d>0, every nonempty original fiber is a singleton and
  the argument gives 2^(-n), stronger than the requested gamma_d/2^n.
- If 0<q<d, changes in affine-span orientation were handled in
  Section 2, and halfspaces constant on a fiber span were handled in
  Section 6. No full d-volume assumption is used.
- Lower-dimensional fibers remain in S throughout; their H_q mass
  is zero when q>0, and they cannot enter G as new integer sections.

For unequal positive intrinsic-volume fibers, M_max/M may be small.
The theorem retains that factor explicitly. It supplies neither a
partition into equally weighted compatible families nor a rule for
combining separate selected centers. Dropping the factor without a
new argument would be an unproved extension to general OC.
